messages.subject: Help with first model, please.
parts:

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Help with first model, please.
parts:
I'm afraid that model's not going to be directly translatable
to Stan, because

* categorical outcomes are integers

* Stan does not allow integer parameters

The only way to work around the restriction on integer parameters
is to marginalize them out as described in the mixture model chapter
of the manual.

The upside is that the models run much faster with the integer
parameters marginalized out than they do sampling in JAGS/BUGS.

Also unlike in BUGS, you don't need to define intermediate
values, and you definitely don't want to define them as parameters.
Defining theta as a parameter is inconsistent with this assignment:
> theta[n,t] <- if_else(n==L[t], 1, 0);

Variables can only be assigned to in the blocks in which they
are defined. But presumably you don't care about theta itself.

So what you need to do is define the log density of p(x) in the
model.

So for your model, all you need to do is remove L and theta
from the parameters declaration (leaving only x) and
calculate p(x[,t] | sigma, pdist) in the inner loop here:

> for (t in 1:T){
> L[t] ~ categorical(pdist);
> for (n in 1:N){
> theta[n,t] <- if_else(n==L[t], 1, 0);
> x[n,t] ~ normal( theta[n,t], Sigma );
> }
> }

I think this will do it in an arithmetically stable way (see
the manual for simpler examples and an explanation of log_sum_exp
and increment_log_prob):
for (t in 1:T) {

vector[N] temp;
temp <- rep_vector(0, N); // fill temp with zeros
for (n in 1:N) {

for (n2 in 1:N) {
temp[n] <- temp[n] + categorical_log(n, pdist)
+ normal_log(x[n2,t], n2 == n, Sigma);
}
}
// temp[n] =def= log p(x[,t] | Sigma, pdist)
increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(temp));
}

Note that (n2 == n) is equal to 1 if they're equal and 0 if
they're not, so you don't need the if_else. And this completely
bypasses the need to define theta.

So the marginalized loop is just calculating:

log p(x[,t] | Sigma, pdist)

= log SUM_n p(x[,t], L[t] == n | Sigma, pdist)

= log SUM_n p(L[t] == n | pdist) * PROD_n p(x[n,t] | L[t])

At least that's my best guess for the marginalization.

I don't understand the model and am just doing the brute
force marginalization. I was very confused by the multiple uses
of N here --- does L have the same number of outcomes as theta
and x's first dimension?

- Bob

parts:
Thanks for the reply. I'll work through your suggestion.

There was a typo, so L was a vector of length T, but it's not the biggest problem.

On each of T trials, a biased N-sided dice is rolled where the bias is given by the simplex (pdist). This then determines the mean (via theta) of a normally distributed variable, x. So the idea was to have observations (x) centred on theta, which is determined by L.

Presumably if I can't use the L output of Categorical as a parameter, I should be able to use this integer output as an array index to look up values in a pre-defined matrix which I can then use as parameters? I've tried to implement this with an ultra minimal example, but it doesn't work. Maybe the differences between STAN and JAGS are greater than I thought, but I would have expected this model would sample values of L, but I still can't get it to parse.

data {
    int<lower=1> N;        // number of spatial locations, N-AFC
    int<lower=1> T;        // number of trials

simplex[N] pdist;       // spatial prior
}
parameters {
    vector[T] L;         // target location on trial n

}
model {
     for (t in 1:T){
         L[t] ~ categorical(pdist);
    }
}
The JAGS equivalent would just be:

model{
for (t in 1:T){

L[t] ~ dcat(pdist)
}

Where pdist would be some predefined vector like [1/3 1/3 1/3]

Thanks for the help.

On Jul 14, 2014, at 7:25 PM, Ben Vincent <drben...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks for the reply. I'll work through your suggestion.
>
> There was a typo, so L was a vector of length T, but it's not the biggest problem.
>

> On each of T trials, a biased N-sided dice is rolled where the bias is given by the simplex (pdist). This then determines the mean (via theta) of a normally distributed variable. So the idea was to have observations centred on theta, which is determined by L.

But the mean is just 0 or 1, right? I still don't quite
get the point of the model, but then I don't have a very
broad experience in modeling.

Maybe someone else could chime in on the model or suggest
alternatives.

> Presumably if I can't use the L output of Categorical as a parameter, I should be able to use this integer output as an array index to look up values in a pre-defined matrix which I can then use as parameters?

The problem is that there isn't an output per se.

A statement like "a ~ foo(b)" just increments the log probability
for the model, it doesn't literally sample a from the foo(b) distribution.
(And by the way, neither does JAGS --- JAGS and BUGS both use the graphical model
structure to compute the Markov blanket of each node, then does
conjugate or non-conjugate Gibbs based on the structure of that blanket.)

> I've tried to implement this with an ultra minimal example, but it doesn't work. Maybe the differences between STAN and JAGS are greater than I thought, but I would have expected this model would sample values of L, but I still can't get it to parse.

Let me emphasize again that the categorical distribution
takes an integer outcome and integers cannot be parameters
in Stan. So the following isn't legal because the type of
L[t] is real, but categorical wants it to be int.

In Stan, the only way to fit a model that has integer
parameters it to marginalize out the integer parameters to
produce a model that's purely continuous.

This can't be done in all cases, but I think the sketch
I gave you earlier should work for this case.

- Bob

parts:
Ok, thanks for your reply, much appreciated. You've answered the core of my question, and I'll see if I can make progress reformulating without the Categorical, following your suggestion. 

It would still be great to hear from someone if the approach I was using in JAGS is just not applicable here. 

The aim is to model how well a person can localise a signal item amongst noise items, over T trials. All observations are noisy, but the signal has a higher mean value (1) than the noise (0). The general approach is to use the same JAGS model twice. 
- The first stage generates some simulated data P(D,x|p,sigma) of locations of the signal (D; sorry this was previously referred to as L) and what noisy observations were made (x), given a prior over the location of the signal and a specific level of observation noise (sigma). 
- The second step is to use this simulated data to see how well true signal locations can be inferred from the noisy observations P(D|x,p,sigma),  given the noisy observations x, the prior over signal location and the observation noise.
- In a third step, outside of JAGS, converts this inferred distribution over D to a best guess (the MAP value) and then compares it to the true vector of signal locations generates in step 1 to calculate the percent correct localisation of the signal.

JAGS model

model{
  for (t in 1:T){
D[t] ~ dcat(pdist)
for (n in 1:N){

theta[n,t] <- ifelse(n==D[t],1,0)
      x[n,t] ~ dnorm(theta[n,t] , 1/variance)
    }
  }
}


I get that theta is an irrelevant intermediate variable here, but I just have it because it is used and affected by other variables in more complex variations of the model.

parts:
On Jul 15, 2014, at 5:53 AM, Ben Vincent <drben...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Ok, thanks for your reply, much appreciated. You've answered the core of my question, and I'll see if I can make progress reformulating without the Categorical, following your suggestion.
>
> It would still be great to hear from someone if the approach I was using in JAGS is just not applicable here.
>
> The aim is to model how well a person can localise a signal item amongst noise items, over T trials. All observations are noisy, but the signal has a higher mean value (1) than the noise (0). The general approach is to use the same JAGS model twice.
> - The first stage generates some simulated data P(D,x|p,sigma) of locations of the signal (D; sorry this was previously referred to as L) and what noisy observations were made (x), given a prior over the location of the signal and a specific level of observation noise (sigma).
> - The second step is to use this simulated data to see how well true signal locations can be inferred from the noisy observations P(D|x,p,sigma), given the noisy observations x, the prior over signal location and the observation noise.
> - In a third step, outside of JAGS, converts this inferred distribution over D to a best guess (the MAP value) and then compares it to the true vector of signal locations generates in step 1 to calculate the percent correct localisation of the signal.

We recommend always doing this step of simulating data
according to the model with known parameters and making sure
those parameters can then be estimated from the data.

Why would you want a posterior mode (aka "MAP", but Andrew hates
that term for some reason) rather than a posterior mean? The
posterior mean has the least expected square error (and a posterior
median has the least expected absolute error). There's no such
decision theoretic interpretation for the MAP.

Also, the typical set (high mass volume of the posterior) doesn't
even contain the max in some cases --- Beta(0.5,0.5) is a good
example to get the general idea of what's going on.

And if you do only want a posterior mode, you might be able to
use Stan's optimization directly rather than MCMC (would depend
on whether there is a maximum likelihood estimate over all parameters
or whether you want a marginal makimum likelihood, which we
should also be supporting in the future).

> JAGS model
>
> model{
> for (t in 1:T){
> D[t] ~ dcat(pdist)
> for (n in 1:N){
> theta[n,t] <- ifelse(n==D[t],1,0)
> x[n,t] ~ dnorm(theta[n,t] , 1/variance)
> }
> }
> }
>
>
> I get that theta is an irrelevant intermediate variable here, but I just have it because it is used and affected by other variables in more complex variations of the model.

Stan lets you declare local variables. It's just a matter
of whether you want to save it or not. If you want to save it,
declare it as a transformed parameter. If you want to just use,
declare it as a local variable in the model block.

And you don't need the ifelse in Stan (and probably in JAGS); you
can just write:

theta[n,t] <- n == D[t];

The == operator returns 1 if the expressions are equal and 0 otherwise.

- Bob
